tour-eiffel: An iron tower 330 metres high, raised for the 1889 World's Fair by the workshops of Gustave Eiffel. It was to stand for twenty years only and became the symbol of Paris. Its three floors can be visited, by lift or by the stairs.
musee-du-louvre: A former palace of the kings of France, turned into a museum in 1793. Its collections run from Antiquity to the middle of the 19th century; visitors come for the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory. The way in is the glass pyramid, opened in 1989.
notre-dame-de-paris: A Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, begun in 1163 and finished nearly two centuries later. Badly damaged by the fire of 2019, it opened again in December 2024 after five years of works.
arc-de-triomphe: An arch 50 metres high, ordered by Napoleon in 1806 and finished in 1836, in the middle of the Place de l'Étoile. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier lies under its vault. Its terrace looks over the twelve avenues that leave the square.
sacre-coeur: A white basilica at the top of the hill of Montmartre, built between 1875 and 1914. Its dome is one of the highest points of Paris.
musee-d-orsay: A museum set in a former railway station, built for the 1900 World's Fair on the bank of the Seine. It shows the art of 1848 to 1914 and one of the largest collections of Impressionist paintings in the world.
palais-de-l-elysee: A mansion built in 1722, the home of the presidents of the French Republic since 1848. It can be visited on Heritage Days only.
centre-pompidou: A centre for art and culture opened in 1977. Its pipes, escalators and frame stand outside the building, painted in bright colours. It houses the national museum of modern art and a large public library.
opera-garnier: An opera house of 1,900 seats designed by Charles Garnier and opened in 1875. Ballets are mostly given there. Its great marble staircase and its ceiling painted by Marc Chagall can be visited during the day.
grand-palais: A large exhibition hall raised for the 1900 World's Fair, under a roof of glass and steel. It hosts exhibitions, fairs and sports events.
pantheon: Built in the 18th century as a church dedicated to Saint Genevieve, the Panthéon became under the Revolution the tomb of the great figures of the nation. Voltaire, Victor Hugo, Marie Curie and Simone Veil rest there.
invalides: A group of buildings ordered by Louis XIV in 1670 to house wounded soldiers. Today it holds the Army Museum and, under its golden dome, the tomb of Napoleon.
jardin-du-luxembourg: A garden of 23 hectares created in 1612 for Marie de' Medici, around the palace where the Senate now sits. It has a large pond where children sail small boats, an orchard, beehives and about a hundred statues.
pere-lachaise: The largest cemetery of Paris, opened in 1804 on a hill in the east of the city. Its paved alleys under the trees lead to the graves of Molière, Chopin, Édith Piaf, Oscar Wilde and Jim Morrison.
sainte-chapelle: A Gothic chapel finished in 1248 to keep the relics brought back by Louis IX. Its fifteen stained-glass windows, 15 metres high, tell the Bible in more than a thousand scenes.
moulin-rouge: A cabaret opened in 1889 at the foot of Montmartre, known by its red windmill. The French cancan was born there.
galeries-lafayette: A department store on Boulevard Haussmann, opened in 1894. Its glass dome of 1912 rises 43 metres above the ground floor, and its terrace looks over the roofs of Paris.
buttes-chaumont: A park of 25 hectares laid out in 1867 in former quarries. A lake surrounds a rocky island topped with a small temple, reached by a suspension bridge. Its slopes are among the steepest of the parks of Paris.
musee-rodin: A museum devoted to the sculptor Auguste Rodin, in the mansion where he worked at the end of his life. The Thinker and the Gates of Hell stand in the garden.
cafe-de-flore: A café of Saint-Germain-des-Prés opened in the 1880s. Writers and philosophers made it their workroom in the 1940s.
bibliotheque-francois-mitterrand: The main site of the national library of France, opened in 1996. Four corner towers shaped like open books stand around a garden of pines, closed to the public. The reading rooms are set around this garden.
notre-dame-de-lorette: A neoclassical church finished in 1836, at the foot of the hill of Montmartre. Its front of columns recalls an ancient temple.
